claim: The abdication itself -- 15 March, at Pskov, after five days of strikes, a garrison mutiny, and a Duma committee that formed to fill the vacuum before anyone had decided it should -- wasn't a decision this government made; it inherited the result.

Power split on arrival between this Cabinet, appointed by the old Duma's committee, and the Petrograd Soviet of Workers' and Soldiers' Deputies, elected in the same chaotic week and controlling the garrison, the railways, and the printing presses this government needs to be obeyed at all.
The Volunteer Army's founders are still serving officers of an army that answers, for now, to this government.
The Czechoslovak Legion is still an Allied unit in transit through Russian territory, over a year from the revolt that will make Siberia a front at all.
The Bolshevik faction inside the Petrograd Soviet is a small, radical minority, not yet the majority that any of this campaign's choices will help build.

Foreign Minister Miliukov's note to the Allies, reaffirming this government's commitment to the war and to the territorial gains the old regime promised itself, has leaked into print exactly as written -- with none of the 'peace without annexations' language the Soviet's own Executive Committee has spent weeks getting this Cabinet to publicly accept.

On 18 May a reorganized coalition cabinet is sworn in with six socialist ministers, Kerensky moving from Justice to War among them -- the first time the Soviet's own people sit in the government rather than merely supervising it from outside.
Every field army and front now has commissars named by the Provisional Government, the Petrograd Soviet and the soldiers' committees.
General Alekseev, the Supreme Commander, will raise the Volunteer Army on the Don after the November rising.
Lenin has been back in Petrograd since 16 April and argues for all power to the Soviets.
The Bolsheviks are a minority in the Soviet.
The Soviet wants the soldiers' rights written into law.
The Soviet's ministers sit in the cabinet and will read whatever you issue.
Brusilov took over as Supreme Commander in late May 1917, when Alekseev was removed.
note: A diary entry of 26 May 1917 records Alekseev's removal; the Old Style or New Style date of the entry is not stated.

claim: Censorship lifted with the old regime, and the range of what Russian newspapers now openly print, from Kadet papers demanding the offensive to Bolshevik ones calling every day of continued war a crime against the men fighting it, is itself something the old empire never had to govern through.
The army's own soldier committees -- elected, and empowered by the Soviet's own Order No. 1 to countermand officers -- are reading all of it.

Brusilov is still Supreme Commander for one more month; the officers who will found the Volunteer Army are watching the front committees test how much authority survives contact with an elected soldier vote.
Still over a year from the Czechoslovak Legion's revolt.

Not yet a command, and not yet arguing this from inside a government -- the Bolsheviks' position that the offensive is a crime against the men fighting it is currently a minority opinion in the Soviet, not yet the policy of anything.

As the new War Minister, you campaigned across the front for this offensive personally, on the argument that Russia keeps its seat among the Allies -- and its claim on any postwar settlement -- only by fighting, not merely by surviving.
The Southwestern Front attacks at dawn on 1 July.

where: roll: The advance stalls in good order
claim: The German-Austrian counterattack on 19 July still breaks the front near Tarnopol, exactly as it did in the record -- committing the reserve doesn't change that.
note: Began 19 July against the 11th Army; Tarnopol fell 25 July.

where: roll: The retreat becomes a rout
claim: The word for what the newspapers do with this by the second week of July is not 'setback.'
Armed soldiers, sailors from Kronstadt, and factory workers are in the streets demanding the Soviet itself take power outright, not merely negotiate with this Cabinet.
The Party's own Central Committee did not order this and is not fully in control of it -- Lenin is not even in the city when it starts.
The garrison units this Cabinet is deciding whether it can even still rely on are, for now, still the same imperial army the Volunteer Army's founders currently still serve in.
The Czechoslovak Legion is still an Allied unit in transit through Russian territory, over a year from the revolt that will make it a front.

For four days the city has been armed and in the streets, and the rising has no single command giving it direction -- which makes it harder to negotiate with and, this Cabinet's staff believe, easier to break, if there are still loyal units left to do the breaking with.
Trotsky is arrested; Lenin, warned in time, goes into hiding and crosses into Finland within days, not returning to the city until October.
The German and Austrian counterattack of 19 July broke the Southwestern Front near Tarnopol.
General Kornilov, who took the Southwestern Front on 21 July, has told the government what he will need as Supreme Commander.
General Denikin commands the Western Front and is about to be given the Southwestern Front that Kornilov is leaving.
Lenin is in hiding after the July Days.
The Soviet's left objects to him.
The State Conference meets in Moscow from 25 August.
Delegates come from the Duma, the Soviets, the army, the banks, the cooperatives and the Cossack hosts.
Kaledin, ataman of the Don Host, speaks for the Cossacks.
The Bolsheviks have called a strike in Moscow against the Conference.
The Conference is the one room in Russia where the generals, the Soviets and the banks sit together.
You open the Conference and speak against both extremes.
The Conference adopts nothing on his program.
The Conference did not settle the split between the government and the generals.
Six weeks ago you made Kornilov Supreme Commander yourself, over the objections of the Soviet's own left, because the front needed someone the officer corps still believed in.
What isn't in dispute: General Krymov's Third Cavalry Corps is moving on Petrograd by rail, and you have just publicly dismissed Kornilov and called it mutiny.

Kornilov never had much use for the Offensive's caution, and says so to anyone who asks -- an army you preferred to consolidate rather than push, in his account, is exactly the kind of army you're now relying on to stop him.
Whether the Party's own moment is still to come depends more on how this crisis resolves than on anything the Central Committee decides on its own this month.
Still over a year from the Czechoslovak Legion's revolt that will make Siberia a front at all.
The Soviet Executive Committee -- including the Bolsheviks you moved against three weeks ago -- is offering to arm every willing hand in the city, Red Guards included, to help stop it.
On 14 September a decree signed by Kerensky proclaims the Russian Republic.
Executive power passes to a Directory of five, with Kerensky as president.
Part of the Soviet Executive Committee wants a government of socialists only.
On 13 September the Petrograd Soviet passed a Bolshevik resolution for the first time.
The Directory is you, Tereshchenko, Verkhovsky, Verderevsky and Nikitin.
note: NOT CONFIRMED by the pages read; widely cited.

claim: The Directory sat from 14 September to 8 October.
note: The page gives 1 (14) September to 24 September (7 October); the cabinet that replaced it was formed 25 September (8 October).

claim: The All-Russian Democratic Conference meets in Petrograd in September.
It votes 766 to 688, with 38 abstentions, for a coalition with the propertied parties.
In letters to the Central Committee he argues that the party should take power.
The Conference has voted for a coalition, narrowly.
A cabinet has to be named that the delegates, the Kadets and the Soviet will all put up with.
On 8 October the new cabinet is sworn in.
note: Six socialist, six liberal and six non-party ministers.

claim: The Directory ended on 8 October, when this cabinet was formed.
At dawn on 6 November cadets arrive to close the plant that prints the Bolshevik newspaper Rabochii Put.
note: 24 October Old Style; the Military Revolutionary Committee ordered it reopened.

claim: The Military Revolutionary Committee of the Petrograd Soviet orders the plant reopened and sends the Lithuanian Regiment and a reserve sapper battalion to guard it.
On 23 October the Bolshevik Central Committee voted ten to two for an armed uprising.
note: 10 October Old Style; not read this round.

claim: The Military Revolutionary Committee was formed in the Petrograd Soviet to control the garrison, and it now has commissars in most regiments.
On the morning of 7 November you leave Petrograd by car for Pskov.
Kerensky spoke to the Pre-Parliament on 6 November and left the capital the next morning.
note: His last speech there; Dan answered.

claim: The Winter Palace was taken in the night of 7 to 8 November.
Whatever this Cabinet did differently through the summer, the rising does not move.

Arming the Soviet's Red Guards to stop Kornilov left several thousand rifles in Bolshevik-organized hands that were never collected back, and a Petrograd Soviet whose Bolshevik share of seats, negligible in May, is now a majority.

On the night of 6–7 November the Military Revolutionary Committee -- a Soviet body, not this Cabinet's -- takes the telephone exchange, the State Bank, the bridges, and the Winter Palace itself by the early hours of 8 November, with barely a shot fired in its actual defense.

Everything the rest of this file's campaigns take as their own opening backstory starts here: the Council of People's Commissars formed that same week; the Constituent Assembly elected in November and dissolved by force in January when it returns a non-Bolshevik majority; Brest-Litovsk signed in March, ceding a quarter of the empire to end a war this government spent this whole campaign trying to keep fighting; and, within weeks of that peace, the civil war that the Armed Forces of South Russia, the Siberian government, and the Revolutionary Military Council fight through 1922.
None of that changes no matter how well or badly this Cabinet is played.
What changes is only how much warning the men who found the Volunteer Army in the Don that winter had, and how isolated a government it was that fell.

Krymov's Third Cavalry Corps was perhaps fifteen thousand men against a capital of over two million -- the real historical margin was that thin, and it held on railway refusals and soldier committees that simply declined to fight, not on any garrison actually stopping the advance by force.
Take the Soviet's Red Guards out of the defense and that thin margin does not hold.

Krymov's Cossacks reach central Petrograd; Kornilov, following behind, is not arrested at Mogilev but is in the capital inside the week, and this Cabinet is not the government that survives the encounter.

Kerensky's own fate in this branch is unresolved by anything the record can settle: arrested alongside the rest of the Cabinet is the most likely outcome contemporaries would have expected, though nothing here should be read as claiming more certainty about that than the record actually supports.

There is no Bolshevik seizure of power in November, because the Petrograd Soviet that would have staged it has just watched a military government take the capital by force with the left's own militia unable or unwilling to stop it.
No Council of People's Commissars, no Brest-Litovsk, no Constituent Assembly dissolved by a Bolshevik decree instead of a Cossack one.
The cabinet takes its fifth emergency decree without the consent of the Soviet Executive Committee.
The fifth has none that the Executive Committee accepts, and it stops sending delegates to the cabinet.
From that day the government rules by ministerial order in Petrograd and nowhere else, and the regiments of the garrison take their orders from the Soviet.
In the record the government never broke with the Soviet in form.
It lost the Soviet's confidence between May and November, a little at a time.

A lawyer and Duma deputy before 1917, the only man to hold high office simultaneously in the Provisional Government and, in its first months, as a deputy chairman of the Petrograd Soviet -- dual power's contradictions embodied in one person rather than argued between two institutions.
Became Minister of War in the first coalition formed after this campaign's opening crisis, then Minister-Chairman from July after the second.

Fled Petrograd by car on 7 November to rally General Krasnov's Cossacks at the front; the counter-attack collapsed at Pulkovo within days, and he never returned to Russian soil in a position of power.

Lived another fifty-three years in exile, mostly in France and the United States, and died in New York in 1970 -- long enough to see nearly the entire war this file's other campaigns describe fought and finished.

An escaped Austrian prisoner of war with a real battlefield reputation, appointed Supreme Commander by Kerensky himself after the Kerensky Offensive's collapse, on Kornilov's own condition that the government back restoring the death penalty and formal discipline at the front.

What exactly Kerensky authorized before Kornilov's own advance on Petrograd in early September is still disputed -- an intermediary, Vladimir Lvov, carried proposals between them that each man afterward described differently, and whether this was a deliberate coup from the start or a plan Kerensky first encouraged and then publicly recast as mutiny is a real historians' argument, not settled the way the coup's failure itself is.

Arrested and held with the other generals implicated at Bykhov Monastery, under a guard lenient enough that he escaped in the chaos of the Bolshevik seizure of power that December, disguised as a Turkoman soldier.

A Georgian Menshevik released from Siberian exile in March 1917, and the real architect of the coalition this campaign's opening crisis produces -- the leading voice of 'revolutionary defencism' (hold the front, seek a negotiated peace without annexations, and work with the Provisional Government rather than against it) against the Soviet's own more radical minority.
The government's ability to speak with the Soviet's actual majority at all runs through him more than through Kerensky.
Opposed the July rising as recklessness that could only help the government's enemies, then opposed the Bolshevik seizure of power in November just as firmly.
Left Russia in 1921 after the Georgian Menshevik republic he helped lead was itself overrun by the Red Army, and died in exile in New York in 1959.

A historian by training and the Kadet (Constitutional Democrat) party's leading figure for two decades before 1917, and the most articulate voice in this Cabinet for the argument that the new government's legitimacy abroad depends on honoring the old empire's commitments, war aims included -- the position the note bearing his name states plainly enough that its publication becomes this campaign's opening crisis.

Remained active in Kadet politics through 1917 and the years after, opposed both the Bolsheviks and, eventually, most of the White movement's own leadership on questions of what postwar Russia should look like, and died in exile in France in 1943.
A Socialist Revolutionary who had organized the assassinations of the interior minister Plehve in 1904 and of Grand Duke Sergei in 1905.
In 1917 he served as a commissar with the army and then as Kerensky's deputy at the War Ministry.
Left the War Ministry in September, after the Kornilov affair.
He fought the Bolsheviks in 1918, lived in exile in Europe, and was arrested after crossing back into the Soviet Union in 1924.
He was sentenced to death, the sentence was reduced to ten years, and he died in the Lubyanka on 7 May 1925.
